title: Is anyone actually shipping full games using AI tools, or is it mostly just speeding up standard pipelines?
author: direvisions
selftext: How are you actually using AI in your day-to-day workflow (coding, shaders, art, narrative, audio)?

comments.author: taisui
comments.body: There are slop hustlers and people who use AI to do the work.  They are different

replies.author: direvisions
replies.body: i think the distinction comes down to how ai is being used. there's a difference between generating something, throwing it into a game, and calling it a finished product versus using ai as a tool to optimize work.

comments.author: Ganiam
comments.body:
My project wasn’t possible until Fable came out. And I’ve used it every week, full usage at 20x, and I’m still possibly a year out before I can show anything.

Most of what I’ve seen is easy slop reminiscent of old shovelware from the 90’s with better graphic

But there has been a few projects here and there that do look good, but there are very few of them and most are not anywhere near ready to be shipped, or the AI was used to speed up some things for people already comfortable with coding

replies.author: direvisions
replies.body: fair point. the accessibility of these tools makes it easy to produce something that looks impressive at first glance, but building an actual game that feels polished, and worth playing is a completely different challenge. i think the real potential of ai in game development is giving smaller studios the ability to pursue projects that would otherwise be unrealistic.

replies.author: hello-xworld
replies.body:
I’m curious why your game is still gonna take a year with AI. Sometimes more time invested does not equal better quality.

Not trying to be an ass, I personally also thought investing more time means more time to refine my game, but I spoke with a very successful indie game dev and they don’t spend more than 8 months per game they release. Obviously this doesn’t apply to every game, but it really got me thinking that perhaps having a tighter deadline means less scope creep, less delays, more movement to get the game shipped

replies.author: Ganiam
replies.body:
My project is pretty big and ambitious, lots of moving parts and multiple dozens of systems that constantly speak to each other every minute or so to decide how hundreds of pieces move independently with billions of potential patterns.

It started off as an experiment to see if I could make something like it happen and I figured I’d work on it until I hit a wall that either the AI or current tech couldn’t handle.

So far it’s been going surprisingly well but my remaining roadmap of ideas is still pretty long. I think I’m about 25% of the way through. The progress has been phenomenal and I’ve been really impressed. But each piece that’s left has a lot of complexity to it still

replies.author: hello-xworld
replies.body: That sounds exciting and interesting. My only suggestion is to make a very limited demo (without revealing too much secret sauce or game loop to avoid copycats) to get feedback. Plus it’ll give you early insight who the target market for your game is. But it sounds cool, best of luck!

replies.author: Ganiam
replies.body:
Thanks!

Yes, I am working up to that. After three months I still have no visual yet, it’s all internal machinerie. I’m excited to see how far I can push it though and I’m going to start working on the playable part sometime in 1-2 months

comments.author: brownDevil9
comments.body: I building from past 2.5 months. I still have a lot more to do. I am maxing out my tokens but still noway near to actual launch. Based on my timing even a MVP is 4 months away at current pace.

comments.author: do-sieg
comments.body: Remove manual repetitive tasks, like setting up a map script, placing characters, starting a cutscene...
